lesson.title: Swallowing the Whole File: The read() Method
lesson.summary: The read() method pulls everything left in an open file into one string in a single call, and calling it again after reaching the end returns an empty string rather than starting over.
lesson.body:
Once a file is open, the most direct way to pull its contents into your program is the `read()` method. Called with no arguments, `file.read()` reads everything left in the file, from wherever the file currently is, all the way to the end, and hands it back as one single string. If the file holds several lines, those lines are not split apart for you, they are still joined together inside that one string, with `"\n"` characters marking where each line break was.

That single detail, that `read()` returns everything as one big string rather than as separate lines, is exactly what the next two chapters build on: `readline()` and `readlines()` exist specifically to give you the file broken into individual lines instead. Reading everything at once with `read()` is simple and works well for files that are not too large, but it does mean the whole file has to fit in memory at once, which is worth keeping in mind for very large files.

```python
file = open("poem.txt", "w")
file.write("Roses are red\nViolets are blue\n")
file.close()

file = open("poem.txt", "r")
contents = file.read()
print(repr(contents))
print(repr(file.read()))
file.close()
```

```python
'Roses are red\nViolets are blue\n'
''
```

This example wraps the results in `repr()` on purpose, so the newline characters show up visibly as `\n` instead of turning into actual line breaks on the screen, which makes it much easier to see exactly what string `read()` produced. The first `read()` call returns the whole file: `'Roses are red\nViolets are blue\n'`, one string containing both lines and both of the newline characters that separate them. Here is the part that trips people up: once `read()` reaches the end of the file, the file remembers that position. Calling `read()` again does not start over from the beginning, it returns an empty string, `''`, because there is nothing left to read. An empty string, not `None` and not an error, is how a file object tells you it has run out of content.
